In this assignment you will work on the data of the **Meltem wind farm**: 12 turbines, 5 years, one record per turbine per day (`meltem_daily.csv`). Read the data dictionary (`meltem_dictionary.md`) first, then look at the data before you compute anything. The four tasks use what we learned in Lectures 4-7: missing values, sampling, time series components and exploratory analysis.

**Rules**

- Do not change anything in this document, other than `student_name` and `student_id` in the chunk above, and the Answer sections below.
- You will submit **only your Rmd file**. I will knit it myself, in a folder that contains `meltem_daily.csv`. So it must run from top to bottom without errors in less than 5 minutes, and it must read the data with the relative file name used in the fixed code. The last chunk of this document collects your objects `imputed` and `split` when it is knitted; knit it yourself first and check that the table at the end shows both.
- Nobody tells you which method to use. Choose your methods, and **explain and justify your choices** in the places marked *Explanation*. A good explanation refers to what you saw in *this* data (a number, a plot) and not to general statements. Generic explanations receive little credit. Respect the word limits.
- Your code must run from top to bottom without errors. Never install new packages. Only the packages we have shown in the course are allowed: `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `readr`, `ggplot2`, `DMwR2`, `mice` and base R.
- You may use AI tools, but you alone are responsible for what you submit. Read the data, and check what the tools do.

**Which data?** `meltem` is the original table as it was given. Only Task 1 produces an imputed table (`imputed`). Tasks 2, 3 and 4 work on the original `meltem`, not on `imputed`: the columns they use (`date`, `turbine`, `fault_next7`, `energy_mwh`, `rotor_rpm`, `gbx_oil_c`) have no gaps, so imputation does not matter there. In Task 1 work on a copy of `meltem` and leave `meltem` itself unchanged.

Good luck!


### Fixed code (do not change)
```{r fixed, cache=F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(readr); library(ggplot2); library(DMwR2); library(mice)
my_seed <- as.numeric(student_id) %% 1000003
meltem  <- read_csv("meltem_daily.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)   # 21,924 rows, 34 columns
dim(meltem)
```


### TASK 1: Missing values (10 points)
`meltem` has missing values. Find all of them and impute them.

Work on a copy of `meltem` and put your result in a data frame named `imputed`, which has the same rows and the same columns as `meltem`. Your imputed values will be compared with the true values (that only the instructor knows): the closer you are, the more points you get. You can lose up to 5 points if you do not explain properly what you did and why.

#### Answer
```{r task1, cache=F}
set.seed(my_seed)
imputed <- meltem                                   # a copy; meltem stays unchanged
rmse <- function(p, a) sqrt(mean((p - a)^2))

# ---- 1. Where are the gaps? ----
colSums(is.na(imputed))[colSums(is.na(imputed)) > 0]
summary(imputed$wind_ms)            # min = -9999: an impossible wind speed, a hidden NA
sum(imputed$wind_ms == -9999)
imputed$wind_ms <- na_if(imputed$wind_ms, -9999)
max(imputed$vib_gbx_mm_s, na.rm = TRUE)   # exactly 9 = the end of the sensor range (dictionary)

# ---- 2. Why are they missing? ----
imputed %>% group_by(month = format(date, "%m")) %>%
  summarise(wind = mean(is.na(wind_ms)), gen_temp = mean(is.na(gen_temp_c)), vib = mean(is.na(vib_gbx_mm_s))) %>%
  mutate(across(-month, ~ round(.x, 3))) %>% print(n = 12)
imputed %>% group_by(gen_temp_missing = is.na(gen_temp_c)) %>% summarise(gen_wind_u_c = mean(gen_wind_u_c), n = n())
imputed %>% group_by(vib_missing = is.na(vib_gbx_mm_s)) %>% summarise(energy_mwh = mean(energy_mwh), gbx_brg_c = mean(gbx_brg_c), n = n())

# ---- 3. Which method is best? Hide known values, impute, compare (Lecture 4) ----
d <- imputed %>% select(where(is.numeric), -fault_next7) %>% as.data.frame()
d$turbine <- factor(imputed$turbine)
gaps <- c("wind_ms", "gen_temp_c", "vib_gbx_mm_s")
hid <- list(wind_ms = sample(which(!is.na(d$wind_ms)), 1000),                       # wind gaps: single days
            gen_temp_c = unlist(lapply(sample(which(!is.na(d$gen_temp_c)), 150), function(i) i:(i + 6))))  # gen gaps: blocks of days
hid$gen_temp_c <- hid$gen_temp_c[hid$gen_temp_c <= nrow(d)]
hid$gen_temp_c <- hid$gen_temp_c[!is.na(d$gen_temp_c[hid$gen_temp_c])]
holed <- d; for (v in names(hid)) holed[[v]][hid[[v]]] <- NA

lm_fill <- function(data, v) {            # regression on all complete columns
  fit <- lm(as.formula(paste(v, "~ . -", paste(setdiff(gaps, v), collapse = " - "))), data)
  predict(fit, data)
}
same_day <- function(res, date) ave(res, date, FUN = function(z) mean(z, na.rm = TRUE))           # other turbines, same day
in_time  <- function(res, turbine) ave(res, turbine, FUN = function(z) approx(seq_along(z), z, seq_along(z), rule = 2)$y)  # neighbouring days

kn <- knnImputation(holed[, names(holed) != "turbine"], k = 10)
mi <- complete(suppressWarnings(mice(holed[, names(holed) != "turbine"], m = 1, method = "pmm", seed = my_seed, printFlag = FALSE)))  # only a note about collinear columns
p_w <- lm_fill(holed, "wind_ms");    r_w <- holed$wind_ms - p_w
p_g <- lm_fill(holed, "gen_temp_c"); r_g <- holed$gen_temp_c - p_g
score <- function(v, p) rmse(p[hid[[v]]], d[[v]][hid[[v]]])
rbind(wind_ms    = c(median = score("wind_ms", median(holed$wind_ms, na.rm = TRUE) + 0 * p_w), knn = score("wind_ms", kn$wind_ms),
                     mice = score("wind_ms", mi$wind_ms), lm = score("wind_ms", p_w), lm_corrected = score("wind_ms", p_w + same_day(r_w, imputed$date))),
      gen_temp_c = c(median = score("gen_temp_c", median(holed$gen_temp_c, na.rm = TRUE) + 0 * p_g), knn = score("gen_temp_c", kn$gen_temp_c),
                     mice = score("gen_temp_c", mi$gen_temp_c), lm = score("gen_temp_c", p_g), lm_corrected = score("gen_temp_c", p_g + in_time(r_g, imputed$turbine)))) %>% round(2)

# vib is cut at 9: test the idea by pretending the sensor stopped at 8
v8 <- d; truth <- v8$vib_gbx_mm_s; cut8 <- !is.na(truth) & truth > 8; v8$vib_gbx_mm_s[cut8] <- NA
p_v8 <- lm_fill(v8, "vib_gbx_mm_s")
c(lm = rmse(p_v8[cut8], truth[cut8]), lm_at_least_8 = rmse(pmax(p_v8, 8)[cut8], truth[cut8]), median_known = rmse(median(v8$vib_gbx_mm_s, na.rm = TRUE), truth[cut8])) %>% round(2)

# ---- 4. Impute with the chosen methods ----
p <- lm_fill(d, "wind_ms")
d$wind_ms <- ifelse(is.na(d$wind_ms), p + same_day(d$wind_ms - p, imputed$date), d$wind_ms)
p <- lm_fill(d, "gen_temp_c")
d$gen_temp_c <- ifelse(is.na(d$gen_temp_c), p + in_time(d$gen_temp_c - p, imputed$turbine), d$gen_temp_c)
p <- lm_fill(d, "vib_gbx_mm_s")
d$vib_gbx_mm_s <- ifelse(is.na(d$vib_gbx_mm_s), pmax(p, 9), d$vib_gbx_mm_s)
summary(d$vib_gbx_mm_s[is.na(imputed$vib_gbx_mm_s)])
imputed[gaps] <- d[gaps]
c(same_dim = identical(dim(imputed), dim(meltem)), any_na = anyNA(imputed))
```

#### Explanation (at most 250 words)
For every column that has gaps: what is the problem with its gaps, which method did you choose and why, and how did you check that your choice is good?

Three columns have gaps. I tested the Lecture 4 methods by hiding known values and comparing them with the truth (RMSE).

**`wind_ms`** has no NAs but 1,113 `-9999` values. These are hidden NAs (an impossible speed), so I used `na_if`. The gaps are MCAR: about 5% in every month. Regression on the complete columns is as good as kNN (0.56 vs 0.55). Turbines on the same day share the same wind, so I added the mean regression residual of the other turbines on that day. On 1,000 hidden values the RMSE is: median 2.07, mice 0.61, kNN 0.55, **regression + same-day correction 0.34**.

**`gen_temp_c`** (1,381 NAs) is MAR: 22% of January and 0% of June is missing, in blocks of days, when the windings are cold (42.6 vs 52.7 °C). A median would be biased. The regression residual of neighbouring days is similar, so I added it, interpolated in time. On hidden 7-day blocks: median 6.99, kNN 1.84, mice 2.15, regression 1.23, **regression + time correction 0.91**.

**`vib_gbx_mm_s`** (990 NAs) is MNAR. The dictionary says the sensor measures 0–9 mm/s, the largest value is exactly 9, and the gaps come on windy summer days (40 vs 18 MWh). These values were above 9. Every method fitted on the known values predicts too low. I checked this by pretending the sensor stopped at 8: the regression RMSE was 0.90 and the median 1.88, but with `pmax(prediction, 8)` it fell to **0.45**. So I filled the gaps with `pmax(regression, 9)`.


### TASK 2: A fair training/test split (6 points)
We want to build a model that predicts the target `fault_next7` from the other columns. You do **not** build the model. Create a training sample and a test sample from the original `meltem` table for this purpose. Start your code with `set.seed(my_seed)`.

Put your result in a data frame named `split` with the three columns `date`, `turbine` and `set`, one row for every `meltem` row that you use, where `set` is `"train"` or `"test"`. Rows that you do not use are simply not in `split`. Your split will be checked for being fair.

#### Answer
```{r task2, cache=F}
set.seed(my_seed)
# rows are not independent (Lecture 6): fault_next7 comes in runs of days
acf(meltem$fault_next7[meltem$turbine == "T01"], lag.max = 14, main = "ACF of fault_next7, turbine T01")
# and all turbines share the same weather on the same day
cor(meltem$energy_mwh[meltem$turbine == "T01"], meltem$energy_mwh[meltem$turbine == "T03"])

# time-ordered split: train = 2020-2023 (past), test = 2024 (future).
# The 7 days before 2024 are not used: their label looks 7 days ahead, into the test year.
test_start <- as.Date("2024-01-01")
split <- meltem %>%
  filter(date < test_start - 7 | date >= test_start) %>%
  mutate(set = ifelse(date >= test_start, "test", "train")) %>%
  select(date, turbine, set)

# checks
split %>% left_join(meltem, by = c("date", "turbine")) %>% group_by(set) %>%
  summarise(rows = n(), share = round(n() / nrow(split), 3), first = min(date), last = max(date),
            turbines = n_distinct(turbine), positives = sum(fault_next7), positive_rate = round(mean(fault_next7), 4))
```

#### Explanation (at most 250 words)
How did you build the two samples, why is this a fair split for *this* data, and which checks did you do?

The rows of this table are not independent (Lecture 6), so a random or stratified row split would not be fair. `fault_next7` comes in runs: one repair makes 7 positive days in a row. The ACF of the target of T01 is 0.86 at lag 1 and only reaches 0 after about 7 days. In a random split, days of the same fault event would land in both sets, and the model would only need to recognise its neighbour day. In addition, all turbines see the same weather (the daily energy of T01 and T03 correlates at 0.93).

So I used a **time-ordered split**: train on the past, test on the future. The test set is the whole year 2024 (4,392 rows, 20.1%), so it covers every season and all 12 turbines. The training set is 2020-01-01 to 2023-12-24 (17,448 rows). I left out the last 7 days of 2023 (84 rows) because their label looks 7 days into the test year and would leak test information. Whole days go to one side.

Checks: both sets contain all 12 turbines, and the dates do not overlap (training ends 2023-12-24, testing starts 2024-01-01). The rare target is present in both sets: 374 positives (2.14%) in training and 70 (1.59%) in testing. So the test set has enough positives to measure recall and precision. The rate is a bit lower in 2024 because that year simply had fewer repairs, which a fair future test must accept.


### TASK 3: Time series components (7 points)
Build the series of the **average daily farm energy per month** from the original `meltem` table: for each day add up `energy_mwh` of the 12 turbines, then average these daily totals within every calendar month. You should get 60 values, from January 2020 to December 2024. As a check, the value of January 2020 is 119.9 MWh per day. Make it a monthly time series (`ts`) and decompose it with `stl`.

Draw the decomposition and evaluate it: what do the trend, the seasonal and the remainder components tell about the farm? Use the autocorrelation function (`acf`) to judge the remainder.

#### Answer
```{r task3, cache=F}
monthly <- meltem %>%
  group_by(date) %>% summarise(farm = sum(energy_mwh)) %>%                    # daily farm total
  group_by(month = format(date, "%Y-%m")) %>% summarise(mwh = mean(farm))     # average per month
nrow(monthly); round(monthly$mwh[1], 1)                                       # 60 values, 119.9

energy_ts <- ts(monthly$mwh, start = c(2020, 1), frequency = 12)
dec <- stl(energy_ts, s.window = "periodic")
plot(dec)

round(dec$time.series[1:12, "seasonal"])                    # seasonal effect, January ... December
round(aggregate(dec$time.series[, "trend"], FUN = mean))    # trend, mean per year
round(apply(dec$time.series, 2, sd), 1)                     # size of the three components

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(energy_ts, main = "ACF: raw series")
acf(dec$time.series[, "remainder"], main = "ACF: remainder")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
round(acf(dec$time.series[, "remainder"], plot = FALSE)$acf[2:4], 2)   # lags 1, 2, 3
```

#### Explanation (at most 250 words)
Describe the trend, the seasonality and the remainder, and say what the `acf` plot shows and what that means.

The series has 60 values, and January 2020 is 119.9 MWh/day. As in the lecture, I used `s.window = "periodic"`: five years are too short to estimate a changing seasonal pattern.

**Seasonality** is the largest component (sd 66.4). It peaks in July (+118) and August (+92) and is lowest in December (−85), so summer and winter differ by about 200 MWh/day. This is the *meltem*, the strong summer wind of the Aegean: the farm produces most of its energy in June–September.

**Trend** (sd 25.5) rises from 189 MWh/day in 2020 to 245 in 2022, then stays flat (246 and 251). Production grew by about 30% in the first three years and then reached a stable level.

**Remainder** (sd 35.1) is not small: it is larger than the trend. Some months are much better or worse than trend plus season, for example unusual weather or turbines out of service.

**ACF.** The raw series shows a seasonal wave with a peak at lag 12 (one year). In the remainder this wave is gone, so the decomposition removed the seasonality. But the remainder is not white noise: lags 2 and 3 are −0.37 and −0.26, outside the blue band. A strong month tends to be followed by weaker months two or three months later. Like the AirPassengers example in Lecture 6, some structure is left in the remainder, so a model of this series should also use past months (lags) and not only trend and season.


### TASK 4: Exploratory analysis (7 points)
The farm has two turbine models with different rated power. The file does not say which turbine has which model. Use the whole original `meltem` table.

**4.1** Find out from the data which turbines belong to the larger model. Draw the plots that show it, and write the ids of the turbines of the larger model in your explanation.

**4.2** Compute the correlation between `rotor_rpm` and `gbx_oil_c` (i) over all rows, (ii) over the rows of the turbines of the larger model, (iii) over the rows of the turbines of the smaller model. Draw one scatter plot of `rotor_rpm` against `gbx_oil_c` that shows the finding.

**4.3** Evaluate your findings.

#### Answer
```{r task4, cache=F}
# 4.1 rated power is the ceiling of the daily energy
per_turbine <- meltem %>% group_by(turbine) %>%
  summarise(max_energy = max(energy_mwh), mean_energy = round(mean(energy_mwh), 1), mean_rpm = round(mean(rotor_rpm), 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(max_energy))
per_turbine
ggplot(meltem, aes(turbine, energy_mwh)) + geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Daily energy per turbine", y = "energy (MWh/day)")
ggplot(meltem, aes(turbine, rotor_rpm)) + geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Rotor speed per turbine", y = "rotor speed (rpm)")
big_ids <- per_turbine$turbine[per_turbine$max_energy > 55]
big_ids

# 4.2 correlations: all rows, then per model
m4 <- meltem %>% mutate(model = ifelse(turbine %in% big_ids, "larger", "smaller"))
round(cor(m4$rotor_rpm, m4$gbx_oil_c), 2)
m4 %>% group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(r = round(cor(rotor_rpm, gbx_oil_c), 2), mean_rpm = round(mean(rotor_rpm), 1), mean_oil = round(mean(gbx_oil_c), 1))
ggplot(m4, aes(rotor_rpm, gbx_oil_c, colour = model)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "black", linetype = 2) +
  labs(title = "Pooled trend (dashed) is negative, the trend within each model is positive",
       x = "rotor speed (rpm)", y = "gearbox oil temperature (°C)")
```

#### Explanation (at most 250 words)
Which turbines are the larger model, and how did you recognise them? What do the three correlations tell about the relation between rotor speed and gearbox oil temperature? What would you tell the maintenance engineers of the farm?

**4.1** The larger model is **T02, T05, T06, T09 and T11**. The rated power is the ceiling of the daily energy. These five turbines reach 64–70 MWh/day, and the other seven stop at 43–48 MWh/day. No turbine falls in between: the energy boxplot shows two groups (a hidden group, Lecture 7). The rotor speed boxplot shows the same five turbines: they turn slowly (mean 6.7–6.9 rpm), and the other seven turn at 10.7–11.1 rpm.

**4.2** Over all rows r = **−0.37**. Within the larger model r = **+0.65** and within the smaller model r = **+0.67**. The sign flips: this is Simpson's reversal. Within each model, a faster rotor (more wind, more load) means hotter gearbox oil. But the larger model turns slowly *and* runs hot (mean oil 66.5 °C at 6.8 rpm), while the smaller model turns fast and runs cool (39.4 °C at 10.9 rpm). This difference between the groups produces the negative pooled trend (dashed line).

**4.3** The pooled correlation is misleading: the model of the turbine is the third variable that explains it. The real relation is positive and almost equal in both models, but the level of the oil temperature depends on the model. Maintenance engineers should judge the gearbox oil temperature **separately for each model**, for example with alarm limits per model and relative to the rotor speed. With one limit for the whole farm, the larger turbines would always look too hot, and an overheating smaller turbine would never be noticed.


### Submission (do not change)
Submit this Rmd file only. When it is knitted, the chunk below collects `imputed` and `split` (it writes `imputed_<your id>.csv` and `split_<your id>.csv`). The table only tells whether the two objects are found in the required format.

```{r final, echo=FALSE}
key3 <- c("date", "turbine", "set")
orig <- read_csv("meltem_daily.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)    # re-read: your own code may have changed `meltem`
imputed <- get0("imputed", ifnotfound = NULL); split <- get0("split", ifnotfound = NULL)
ok_imp <- is.data.frame(imputed) && nrow(imputed) == nrow(orig) && all(names(orig) %in% names(imputed))
ok_spl <- is.data.frame(split) && all(key3 %in% names(split)) && nrow(split) > 0 && all(split$set %in% c("train", "test"))
if (ok_imp) write.csv(imputed[, names(orig)], paste0("imputed_", student_id, ".csv"), row.names = FALSE)
if (ok_spl) write.csv(split[, key3], paste0("split_", student_id, ".csv"), row.names = FALSE)
kable(data.frame(item = c("Task 1: `imputed` is ready", "Task 2: `split` is ready"), status = c(ifelse(ok_imp, "yes", "NO"), ifelse(ok_spl, "yes", "NO"))))
```
